reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign minor salivary gland adenoma with a striking predilection for the upper lip, and less commonly the buccal mucosa.
It typically affects older adults with a slight female predominance and presents as a slow-growing, submucosal, painless nodule.
The histological hallmark is columnar to cuboidal cells arranged in single or double branching, anastomosing cords that periodically separate to form bead-like canaliculi.
The stroma is characteristically loose, hypocellular and richly vascular, unlike the stroma of basal cell adenoma.
Multifocality is well recognised and can present as several discrete nodules within the upper lip.
In contrast to most salivary tumours, it lacks a true myoepithelial component; tumour cells are S100 positive and often bcl-2 positive.
It is readily mistaken clinically for a mucocele of the upper lip, but its solid nature at excision distinguishes it.
The principal serious differential is adenoid cystic carcinoma, which the cords and canaliculi can superficially resemble on small biopsies.
reference.pathophysiology: Canalicular adenoma is a benign neoplasm arising from the ductal (luminal) epithelial cells of minor salivary glands, most typically those of the upper lip. The neoplastic columnar cells retain ductal differentiation and are notable for the absence of a neoplastic myoepithelial population, which sets it apart from pleomorphic and basal cell adenomas. The tumour cells form long, branching, anastomosing cords that intermittently draw apart to create elongated canalicular lumina, set within a conspicuously loose and highly vascularised stroma that is prone to haemorrhage and cystic change. Its frequent multifocality within the upper lip suggests a field origin from multiple minor gland ducts rather than a single clonal focus.
additionalInvestigations: Incisional or excisional biopsy for definitive histology
Fine-needle aspiration cytology (of limited value in the lip)
Ultrasound of the lip or cheek where useful
MRI for larger or deeper lesions to assess extent
Clinical examination of other minor gland sites for multifocal nodules
redFlags: Infiltrative growth or ill-defined margins on histology
Perineural symptoms such as numbness suggesting a malignant mimic
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as the tumour is benign and local excision is curative. Apparent recurrence usually reflects a separate multifocal nodule rather than incomplete removal.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as adenoid cystic carcinoma on a small or fragmented biopsy
Overlooking multifocal nodules within the upper lip
Mistaking it clinically for a simple mucocele and delaying excision
Proceeding to overly aggressive surgery for a benign lesion
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
Gnepp's Diagnostic Surgical Pathology of the Head and Neck
Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Confirm the diagnosis histologically, distinguishing it from basal cell and pleomorphic adenoma
Treat with complete conservative local excision, which is curative for this benign tumour
Inspect the upper lip for multifocal nodules and excise coexisting lesions at the same time
Keep excision margins minimal given the benign nature, avoiding overtreatment
Follow up clinically, recognising that a new nodule usually represents separate multifocal disease rather than true recurrence
